standard.title: Repeating Patterns
standard.description: recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns represented in different ways
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have informal experience noticing and creating patterns in play (e.g. arranging blocks in a sequence, singing songs with repetition). They have not yet formally identified or described the repeating unit in a pattern, or continued a pattern beyond what they can see.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns represented in different ways, describing the repeating unit.

nodes.label: Noticing repetition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that a pattern repeats and point to where the repetition occurs.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of a repeating pattern using materials or shapes, and say 'it repeats'.
nodes.typical_width: Identify repeating patterns across materials, shapes, sounds and movements; point to the part that repeats and say what comes next.
wider: Identify repeating patterns in images generated by dynamic geometric software or a generative AI tool
Identify repeating patterns observed on Country/Place and in First Nations Australians' artwork and material cultures (e.g. shell and seed necklaces)

response_modes.reason: Students at Foundation often confuse a 'pattern' with any arrangement. Encountering repeating patterns across multiple sensory modalities (visual, auditory, movement) helps them isolate the defining feature — repetition of a unit — rather than pattern meaning 'colourful' or 'organised'. Breadth across representation types is what resolves this confusion.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Patterns appear richly across materials, sound, movement, and cultural contexts. Advancing students can explore the same principle of repetition across very different sensory and cultural domains — each new domain gives a fresh angle on what 'repeating' means.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate 'pattern' with any arrangement cannot identify the repeating unit — the concept nodes 2 and 3 require. Without unit identification, copying becomes visual mimicry and continuing becomes guessing, not algebraic reasoning.
success_criteria: Student points to the part of a pattern that repeats and states that it repeats
Student identifies at least one pattern represented in two different ways (e.g. colours and shapes)

nodes.label: Copying a pattern
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can copy a repeating pattern using the same or different materials.
nodes.minimum_width: Copy one repeating pattern (e.g. red-blue-red-blue) using the same materials as the original.
nodes.typical_width: Copy repeating patterns using a range of materials, shapes, sounds and movements; copy patterns made with materials using a different medium (e.g. copy a bead pattern with stamps).
wider: Copy repeating patterns from First Nations Australians' artworks or cultural objects using art materials
Copy a movement or sound pattern (e.g. drumbeats or dance moves) and transfer it to a different medium (e.g. draw the sound pattern)

response_modes.reason: Accurate copying requires careful one-to-one attention to the repeating unit. Students commonly copy an incomplete unit or lose track mid-copy. Repeated practice with the same and different materials builds the precision needed before continuing patterns.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot accurately reproduce a repeating unit cannot continue one — node 3 depends on students holding the unit in mind precisely enough to project it forward. Inaccurate copying produces patterns with a defective unit, making continuation unreliable.
success_criteria: Student produces an accurate copy of a repeating pattern with at least two full repetitions of the unit
Student matches the order and type of elements in the original pattern

nodes.label: Continuing a pattern
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can continue a repeating pattern by identifying what comes next.
nodes.minimum_width: Continue a given repeating pattern by adding at least two more elements, explaining what comes next.
nodes.typical_width: Continue repeating patterns of two or more elements represented in different ways; describe what comes next and why; connect pattern continuation to familiar routines (e.g. setting a table, a repeated song).
wider: Continue and describe repeating patterns from First Nations Australians' cultural contexts (e.g. continuing a pattern from a dance, song or artwork)
Create an original repeating pattern and invite a partner to continue it — explaining the rule to check their partner's response
Continue patterns involving more than two alternating elements, describing the repeating unit

response_modes.reason: Continuing a pattern requires students to have identified the repeating unit, not just the surface feature. Patterns that look familiar (only two alternating colours) can be continued by guessing without understanding the unit. Broader contexts — sounds, movements, mixed-attribute patterns — require students to isolate and apply the repeating rule rather than pattern-match by surface similarity.

This node integrates recognising (node 1) and copying (node 2) into productive use — students must hold the repeating unit in mind and project it forward. The coordination of noticing and reproducing is the key learning here.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Pattern continuation in varied contexts — across sounds, movements and cultural patterns — is where the generalised idea of a repeating rule becomes clear to students. Rich width here deepens the algebraic foundation for later pattern description and generalisation.
success_criteria: Student correctly extends a pattern by at least two elements and explains what element comes next
Student can identify the repeating unit in the pattern they have continued
